question: What is a generator in Python and why would you use one?
key_points: uses yield to produce values
produces values lazily, one at a time
saves memory compared to building a full list
can only be iterated once
answer: A generator is a function that uses yield instead of return. Each time you ask for the next item it runs until the next yield, so values are produced lazily, one at a time. That saves memory because you never build the whole list. Once it is used up you can't loop over it again.
note: Says all four ideas plainly.

question: What does it mean for an HTTP method to be idempotent? Give examples.
key_points: calling it many times has the same effect as calling it once
PUT and DELETE are idempotent
POST is not idempotent
it matters because requests get retried
answer: Idempotent means repeating the request has the same effect as doing it once. PUT and DELETE are idempotent; POST isn't, because two POSTs can create two orders. It matters because clients and proxies retry requests after a timeout.
note: All four, with an example.

answer: It means sending the same request twice leaves the server in the same state as sending it once. That is why a client can safely retry it after a timeout.

question: How do Kafka consumer groups work?
key_points: consumers in a group share the partitions of a topic
each partition is read by only one consumer in the group
a consumer joining or leaving triggers a rebalance
different groups each get every message
answer: A consumer group is a set of consumers that split a topic's partitions between them, and inside one group a partition goes to exactly one consumer. When a consumer joins or crashes, Kafka rebalances and hands its partitions to the others. A second group reading the same topic gets its own full copy of every message.
note: All four.

note: Only the one-consumer-per-partition rule.

question: What is a database index, and what does it cost?
key_points: a data structure (often a B-tree) that speeds up lookups
it avoids scanning the whole table
it slows down writes because the index must be updated too
it uses extra storage
answer: An index is usually a B-tree kept next to the table, so the database can jump straight to the rows instead of scanning everything. The price is slower inserts and updates, since every write must also update the index.
note: Strong, but never mentions storage.

question: Explain retrieval-augmented generation (RAG).
key_points: documents are split into chunks and turned into vectors (embeddings)
the question is embedded and the most similar chunks are retrieved
the retrieved chunks are added to the prompt as context
it reduces hallucination and lets the answer cite sources
answer: You split the documents into chunks and embed each one as a vector. At question time you embed the question too and fetch the most similar chunks. Those chunks go into the prompt as context, so the model answers from real text, hallucinates less, and can cite the page it used.
note: All four.

question: What is the time complexity of looking up a key in a hash map, and when can it get worse?
key_points: average lookup is O(1)
the worst case is O(n) when many keys collide
a good hash function and resizing keep it close to O(1)
answer: On average it's O(1). If many keys land in the same bucket it degrades to O(n) in the worst case. A good hash function plus resizing the table when it fills up keeps lookups near O(1).
note: All three.

question: What are common cache invalidation strategies?
key_points: time-to-live (TTL) expiry
write-through: update the cache when the database is written
cache-aside: the app loads data into the cache on a miss
evicting least recently used (LRU) items when full
answer: Usually you give each entry a TTL so it expires on its own, and when the cache is full you throw out the least recently used items.
note: TTL and LRU only.

question: What does the temperature setting do in an LLM?
key_points: it controls how random the output is
a low temperature gives focused, repeatable answers
a high temperature gives more creative, varied answers
answer: Temperature controls how random the sampling is. Near zero the model picks the most likely words, so answers are focused and repeatable; higher values make it more creative and varied.
note: All three.
